written.q: Define virtualization and a hypervisor. Why is virtualization called the core enabling technology of the cloud? (5 marks)
written.a: Virtualization creates a software-based version of a resource (server, storage, network, OS) so one physical machine behaves like several independent machines. A hypervisor (virtual machine monitor) is software that creates, runs and manages VMs, sitting between hardware and VMs, allocating CPU, memory, storage and network and isolating the VMs. It is the core enabler because nearly every cloud service runs on a virtualization layer that shares physical hardware across many customers, enabling resource pooling, multi-tenancy, rapid provisioning and elasticity.

written.q: Compare Type 1 and Type 2 hypervisors with examples. (8)
written.a: Type 1 (bare-metal) runs directly on the hardware with no host OS: near-native performance, smaller attack surface, more involved installation, used in data centres and clouds (ESXi, Hyper-V, Xen, KVM). Type 2 (hosted) runs as an application on a host OS: easy to install, but lower performance because calls pass through the host OS, and it inherits host OS vulnerabilities; used on developer laptops for testing and sandboxing (VirtualBox, VMware Workstation, Parallels).

written.q: Explain how a hypervisor virtualizes CPU, memory and I/O. (6)
written.a: CPU: physical cores are time-sliced and scheduled across virtual CPUs given to each VM. Memory: physical RAM is partitioned and mapped so each VM has its own isolated address space. I/O: virtual NICs and virtual disks stand in for physical devices and translate VM requests to the real hardware.

Server: many virtual servers with their own OSes on one physical server (consolidation, isolation). Storage: physical storage pooled into one logical resource (simpler management, snapshots, replication, thin provisioning). Network: virtual switches, VLANs and SDN abstract the network so it can be changed in software. Desktop: desktop OSes run centrally and are delivered remotely (VDI).

written.q: Give the benefits and limitations of virtualization. (6)
written.a: Benefits: better utilisation, cost savings (hardware, power, cooling), faster provisioning, easier disaster recovery through snapshots/images. Limitations: hypervisor performance overhead, licensing complexity, the host/hypervisor is a single point of failure for all its VMs, and a compromised hypervisor exposes all VMs (hyperjacking).

written.q: Compare VMs and containers on isolation, size, boot time, density and use. When would you choose each? (8)
written.a: VMs: strong isolation (separate kernel), GBs, minutes to boot, lower density, used for strict isolation and mixed OS needs. Containers: weaker isolation (shared kernel), MBs, seconds to start, higher density, used for microservices, fast scaling and CI/CD. Choose VMs for hardware-level isolation, different guest OSes, legacy apps needing a full OS, and multi-tenant security. Choose containers for microservices, fast startup and density, CI/CD pipelines and rapid horizontal scaling.

written.q: Why do cloud providers run containers inside VMs? (3)
written.a: The VM provides strong, hardware-enforced isolation between tenants, while containers inside it provide fast, efficient deployment — combining the security of VMs with the agility of containers.

written.q: Explain regions, availability zones, resource pooling and multi-tenancy. (8)
written.a: A region is a geographic area containing several availability zones. Each AZ has independent power, cooling and networking and is an isolated failure domain, so workloads spread across AZs survive a facility failure. Resource pooling combines compute, storage and network into a shared pool through virtualization, from which a scheduler allocates on-demand slices. Multi-tenancy means many customers share the same infrastructure with isolation enforced in software, giving economies of scale and low pay-as-you-go prices.

written.q: Describe the four layers of cloud architecture. (4)
written.a: Physical infrastructure (servers, storage, networking, power, cooling) → virtualization layer (hypervisors and container engines pool and allocate) → orchestration and management (schedulers decide placement, scaling, recovery) → service layer (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS consumed by customers).
